We don’t know where any next step leads. We can’t see beyond the next corner. But we also don’t need to. We just have to take it, and then we’ll see what happens. What follows could be a dead end. It could be a new beginning. But we won’t know unless we venture out and take that next step.
The next breath is enough. Everything you need is always right in front of you. You just have to trust that it’s there, and then you’ll see it.

### Title: Heading Out for a Bit

### Content: 
Samurai Champloo is an anime classic set in Japan’s Edo period, a time of shoguns, samurai, and strict social order. The story follows three unlikely friends: Fuu, a young waitress from a teahouse, Mugen, a short-tempered outlaw, and Jin, a quiet, disgraced samurai, aka ronin.
One of Jin’s most notable habits is that whenever he leaves the group, even if only for a short time, he’ll simply say, “Heading out for a bit.” No explanation. No hint as to where he’s going or when he’ll be back. Just a statement of his departure, and off he goes.
Jin is a ronin not just because he lost his master but because he chose to be a lone wolf. He’s not used to having friends, let alone traveling with them. That’s why he doesn’t understand the concept of “I’ll be back in 20 minutes.” He doesn’t know he needs to give them a heads up.
As the show goes on, Jin gets more comfortable with his friends. He’ll sometimes volunteer where he’s going. Occasionally, he even asks for company. But he never loses his habit of “heading out for a bit.”
I’ve been a lone wolf for a long time. I don’t always remember to tell people when I’m leaving, and I definitely suck at saying goodbye. But I’m getting better. I now try to let people know when I’m going on vacation, and I even manage to say “bye for now” on my email newsletter every once in a while.
The older I get, the more “tribes” I’m a part of. I have a family. I have a girlfriend. I have readers, and I have friends. It’s important to feel like you belong, but it’s also important to have time on your own. To think. To wander. To recharge. And when you need that time, you can just say, “Heading out for a bit.”
It’s okay to be a lone wolf. Just don’t forget to come back.

### Title: Calculated Moves

### Content: 
A new LinkedIn connection sent me a nice compliment. I thanked him, gave him my email, and we briefly went back and forth. He asked to speak more, but when I offered him a 20-minute chat on a weekday, which, given my full-time job, is a lot, he said: “Oh, that’s not really enough for a proper presentation.”
“Wait a minute,” I thought. “Are you trying to sell me something?” It seems so. He even has a proper marketing website for his new tool, complete with a pricing page. The problem is he never said a word about it. He just wanted to “talk.” I’m sure he’s proud of his new creation, and I’m happy to consider it, but if you want to sell me something, just say you want to sell me something. Don’t beat around the bush. That’s not how business works.
The only reason to make calculated moves in business is to save time and money. If you know you can save 20% on a deal by approaching the seller through a back channel, that’s a smart move. If you want to get someone to buy your product, however, the only way to do it is to show up and say: “Hey! I made this. I think it’s great, and I hope you will too. Do you want to buy it?” That’s it. There’s no other way. Everything else is a detour, and if you take too many of those, you’ll never reach your goal.
If you want to sell something, sell it. If you want to collaborate, suggest a collaboration. And if you want to get to know someone, just say hi. There’s nothing wrong with being professional, but if professionalism means you can’t be authentic, you’re doing it wrong. Don’t make calculated moves when life requires an honest approach.

### Title: Nourishing in Increments

### Content: 
One theme in Samurai Champloo is hunger. The protagonist, a teenage girl named Fuu, and her companions—two bickering swordsmen—are mainly trying to make it from meal to meal in feudal Japan.
 but also “hunger,” Fuu will often say. “I’m hungry,” “he’s hungry,” “we’re all hungry.” It’s a running joke in the show, but it’s also a theme that permeates the whole story.
When the trio first meets, Fuu is starving. She’s a waitress in a tea house, and her boss won’t let her eat. When she does, she eats in increments. One stolen onigiri here, a few leftover scraps there. It’s only after she runs away with the two samurai that she gets to eat a proper meal.
The same applies to her dream of finding “the samurai who smells of sunflowers.” She can’t accomplish it in a day. She must do it one step at a time. And even though they don’t always get along, her two new friends also seem to be hungry for something. A home. A purpose. A sense of meaning. And so the three of them travel together.
Sometimes, the gang will have a lucky streak. They’ll find a kind merchant who feeds them, or they’ll earn some coin doing odd jobs. But they never get too far before their pockets and bellies are empty again. In one episode, they even win a huge amount of money, but it gets stolen before they can enjoy it.
When I started my first job, I thought I’d finally be set. I was so sick of being a broke college student. I would spend my weekends working at a call center, and I’d spend the money on a 2-euro slice of pizza. It was a far cry from the lifestyle I wanted to have. But even though my salary was 60x what I made in that call center, it still didn’t last very long. I could pay my rent, sure, but I couldn’t buy a car, nor could I travel the world. I was still hungry.
In a way, we are all hungry. Not just for food or money but for meaning, connection, and impact. These things, too, we can only attain in increments. A great meal won’t last you a week, and a big payday won’t last you a lifetime. In the same vein, a single painting won’t make you feel like a great artist, and neither will a single compliment from a fan.
It’s hard to accept that we’ll always be hungry. That there’ll always be something more to want, more to attain, more to feel, understand, and experience. But it’s also comforting. There’s always another meal to be had, another trip to be taken, another person to meet. We’ll never be done, but we’ll also never be bored.
Life is about nourishing yourself in increments. Some days you’ll have a feast, and on others you’ll be starving. Enjoy the former when you can, and endure the latter until it changes. After all, you’re not alone. We’re all hungry—but we’re also all in it together.

### Title: The Painter Who Couldn’t See

### Content: 
There once was a painter who couldn’t see. He wasn’t born blind. In fact, he enjoyed the gift of vision for the first 68 years of his life. Once he developed cataracts, however, the sense he relied most on to make his art began to darken—and so did his paintings.
James McNeill Whistler was an American expat who spent most of his life in the UK. He was known for his moody paintings and witty, often provocative remarks. “The vast majority of English folk,” he said, “cannot and will not consider a picture as a picture, apart from any story it may be supposed to tell.” Whistler demanded people view art for its own sake, not as a means to an end.
After his mother died in 1881, Whistler’s paintings grew darker still. He painted a lot of seascapes, nocturnes, and cityscapes shrouded in fog. He received many awards for his work, including an honorary membership in the Royal Academy of Arts, which he declined.
In 1903, Whistler died in London. He was 69 years old. His eyesight had been deteriorating for years, but his last painting was finished only a few months before his death. It was a seascape, of course. A dark painting made by a painter who couldn’t see.

### Title: It’s Not Time To Worry Yet

### Content: 
When lawyer Atticus Finch is tasked with defending a Black man in 1933 Alabama, for the first time, the single dad to two preteens is forced to put his children through something they won’t understand. For months, they’ll have to endure the misgiving looks and hateful comments from all around town. Never mind the fact that the defendant is innocent. People believe what they want to believe.
“Do you really think there’s a chance, Atticus?” his daughter Scout asks him. “Well, if I didn’t, I couldn’t live in this town,” he responds. “I couldn’t hold my head up.” “Do you think they’ll take Tom Robinson’s life?” “I don’t know, Scout.” And then, as if he was talking to himself, Atticus goes on: “I don’t know, but I gotta do it. I couldn’t go to church and worship God if I didn’t try to help that man.”
As the trial gets underway, Atticus is called “nigger-lover” in the street. His children are beaten up by their school friends. It’s all very stressful, but through it all, Atticus maintains a kind yet stern face. “I’m not worried yet,” he tells his brother. “I want to keep this in perspective.” And when his daughter tells him she’s not sure she can take any more of the insults, he simply reminds her: “You just hold your head high, and keep those fists down.”
It’s easy to let our troubles get to us. To worry about the worry before the worry has even begun. But Atticus Finch reminds us that it’s not time to worry yet. There’s no need to get worked up over a future that might not happen. Only time will tell, and time is something we all have as long as we’re alive.
Stay in the moment. Keep your head high, and your fists down. There’s always a chance tomorrow will be a good day — and until it’s over, so are you.

### Title: The Eternity Mindset

### Content: 
I’m writing this blog in 23 minutes, but I try to believe I have all the time in the world.
 but can’t, don’t, gonna, have to, how, if, just, maybe, might, must, need, no, not, or, perhaps, should, so, stop, supposed to, want, what, when, where, why, will, won’t, would, yeah, yes, you.
I’m writing this blog in 23 minutes, but I try to believe I have all the time in the world. That’s what it feels like when you have a mission. You’re not worried about the details. You’re not worried about the timeline. You know you’ll get there eventually, so you just keep driving.
You don’t need a map. You don’t need directions. You don’t need to know how you’ll navigate the next turn. You just need to keep going. You need to keep driving. The path will unfold in front of you. You’ll know the next exit to take when you get there.
The only way to waste your time is to stop driving. To throw your hands up in the air and say, “I don’t know what to do.” That’s a lie. You always know what to do. You always know the next step. The next step might be a wrong turn, but even that will lead you somewhere. You can always come back. You can always try something else. You can always U-turn and take a different exit.
What you can’t do is stop driving. You can’t let the car sit idle. You can’t drift along at one mile per hour. You need to keep driving. You need to go fast. You need to go fast so you can take the turns. You need to go fast so you can go far. You need to go fast so you can take wrong turns, U-turn, and find the right path. You need to go fast so you can have a real mission. So you can feel like you have all the time in the world.
The only way to waste your time is to stop driving. Don’t stop driving.

### Title: No Time To Explain

### Content: 
In July 2010, someone on the BitcoinTalk forum challenged Satoshi Nakamoto on the scalability of his experimental, peer-to-peer payment network. After several users discussed the issue, Satoshi eventually weighed in, addressing some assumptions and pointing to a prior post for more of his thoughts on the topic. He ended his entry with a line that has been making the rounds in the crypto community ever since: “If you don’t believe me or don’t get it, I don’t have time to try to convince you, sorry.”
More than a decade later, Bitcoin has proven itself to many, but not all. The joke is that, to this day, Satoshi still hasn’t returned to try and convince us. He was the last one to believe in the technology he had created, and then, he was gone. No time to explain. It was up to the rest of us to figure out the rest.
In a world where everyone must sell themselves on social media 24/7, it’s easy to forget: The best things usually sell themselves. They might not do so immediately, but if you’re too busy to explain, perhaps that’s a good thing. It means you’re doing. Creating. Trying to make something so good it won’t need a lot of explaining.
If you have to twist people’s arms to get them to buy your product, read your article, or listen to your song, perhaps it’s not the right product, article, or song. A good cause will attract many followers. A bad one won’t find any, no matter how much you yell.
Choose quality over marketing, and if you don’t believe me or don’t get it, I don’t have time to try to convince you, sorry.

### Title: Important Ideas Will Come Back

### Content: 
I used to regret not writing down ideas for posts that came to me at night. I wanted to hold on to every flash of insight. Even back then, rationally, I knew most of my ideas wouldn’t be great, but I thought, “Hey, if I don’t ship all of them, how will I ever find out which ones resonate with people?”
Now, I realize that if I don’t remember an idea in the morning, it probably wasn’t all that important. If it was, I would have remembered it. I would still have the idea. That’s what it means to be important: you can’t shake it. It lingers. It stays. It keeps coming back.
The best ideas are like songs: If the lyrics are important to you, you’ll remember them. You’ll hum along at work, and at night, you’ll dream about them. You’ll wake up with a melody and go, “Oh yeah! That’s the one!”
If an idea is important to you, it will keep coming back. You’ll find yourself thinking about it again and again. It’ll pop up in your mind at random times, and each time, you’ll get a little more clarity. A little more confidence. You’ll trust the idea a bit more. Until, one day, you’ll know it’s ready. You’ll feel it in your bones. That’s when you can write the post, give the talk, or start the company.
If you can’t remember an idea in the morning, it probably wasn’t all that important. If it was, it would have come back.

### Title: Engaged

### Content: 
The word “engaged” means a lot of things. For one, it means “busy.” “Occupied.” “Already in use.” By the time you agree to marry someone, that sure will be the case. You’ll already have seen your fair share of love. With each other. With the others. But now, you agree to hold out for someone special, and, in the meantime, no one else shall take that special place.
But “engaged” also means “interested.” “Curious.” “Excited.” That’s what you’ll have to be for your relationship to last. After all, “engaged” is what we are when we attend a wedding. The event itself. It’s a ceremony, and then, it’s a state of mind. That state, too, is what the couple must maintain. They must keep their interest in one another. Stay curious. And get excited every time they see each other.
Finally, “engaged” also means “involved.” “Participating.” “Fully present.” That’s the kind of partner we all hope for, isn’t it? Someone who’s 100% there, ready to give their best, ready to face whatever might come. Someone who’s willing to be part of the solution, not the problem. Someone who’ll be as engaged in the marriage as they were in the dating.
“Engaged” means a lot of things. The question is will you be any of them? Not just in your relationship, of course, but in life. Because it’s not just a great way to approach love. It’s a great way to live.
Engaged. It’s a state of being, not just a state of romance. Make sure you’re in it, and not just on Valentine’s Day.

### Title: The Kind of Letter You Want To Receive

### Content: 
“Maybe we are both idiots?” The words were staring back at me from a postcard. The paper was printed in Italy, but it was written on in German—by a guy in Poland, naturally. My friend Robert—aka Multithink —truly lives up to his online alias.
 as in “maybe,” not as in “idiot,” of course. The question was in reference to a book I’d recommended to him, The War of Art. It’s Steven Pressfield’s take on overcoming creative resistance, and it’s a book I can read again and again. “I’m reading it for the third time,” I told him. “Maybe we are both idiots, reading the same book three times,” he thought. Or maybe we’re just stubborn. Maybe we just want to get better at our craft. Maybe we’re not idiots at all.
I’m sure there’s a lesson in here about how much you can say in how few words, but the real reason I’m telling you this story is that it’s the kind of letter you want to receive. The kind you can’t help but smile about. The kind that makes you think, “I’m glad I opened my mailbox today.”
In a world where the mailman mostly brings bills, advertisements, and other bad news, it’s easy to feel that checking your mailbox is a chore. But it shouldn’t be. That’s not what mail is for.
When I was younger, I used to send and receive postcards all the time. I had a map on which I marked all the places I’d been, and I’d always send a card back home. I also collected them from friends, family, and other people I knew. I must have 100 postcards and counting. Somewhere. Nowadays, I rarely send any. Maybe I should change that.
The last time I checked, it only cost 45 cents to send a postcard within Germany. That’s a bargain for a moment of joy. If you can make someone’s day for 45 cents plus five minutes of your time, why wouldn’t you?
I’m not saying you should send a postcard to everyone you know every day. That’s not feasible, and it’ll quickly get expensive. But every now and then, a handwritten note can go a long way. And if you’re not the recipient, it might as well be the sender.
The next time you open your mailbox and go, “Ugh, more boring mail,” ask yourself: “When’s the last time I sent something that wasn’t?” Chances are, you’re not the only one wishing for the kind of letter you want to receive.

### Title: Tainted Material

### Content: 
Despite recently descaling our electric kettle, its filter kept clogging up. After each boil, the hot water would only drizzle out in spurts. “What’s with this thing?” I thought, “I just cleaned it!” I took out the filter at the spout, rubbed it, shook it, and put it back.
I repeated this process several times, and it always helped a little, but never for long. Eventually, I realized that the particles in the filter were too fine to be removed by hand. I took the filter apart, and sure enough, I found sand. Not much, but enough to clog the fine mesh.
I rinsed the filter under running water, and it was back to its usual self. I’ve had to repeat the process several times since, and it’s taught me a valuable lesson: Sometimes, the source of tainted material is tainted material.
When a project goes wrong, you can try to fix it in different ways. You can make a small change to the final result, or you can adjust the process. You can change the process a little, or you can change it a lot. You can also scrap the project altogether, but that’s not the end of it.
If you decide to restart the project, you can begin from the same place you started the first time, or you can begin from a different place. You can use the same materials, or you can use different materials. You can even choose different people to work on the project, and you can change the timeline.
If you’re a creative, you’ll likely be familiar with this particular crossroads in the road: “Do I keep editing the video, or do I re-record it?” If you’re a manager, you’ll face a similar question: “Do I give the team more time, or do I give them a new deadline?”
The answer to these questions is not always obvious, and it’s rarely black and white. You can edit the video and re-record some scenes. You can give the team a new deadline but also a little more time. But when you’re stumped, when you’ve tried every trick in the book, and nothing seems to work, consider tainted material. Perhaps it’s time to throw out the sand, clean the filter, and start over.
It’s not an option we should turn to first, but it sure is liberating to remember it’s there.

### Title: What Do You Not Want To Do Today?

### Content: 
We were sipping on preposterous, eight-euro tea in the Four Seasons lobby when my friend Michael walked me through his daily journaling prompts.
’t’s: “What do you want to do today?”
“It’s a good question,” I said, “but I think I might flip it around: What do you not want to do today?”
The reason I’m less excited about Michael’s original prompt is that, every morning, I already know what I want to do. I want to write. I want to work on the book. I want to think about the business. I want to send out a newsletter, an email, and make a sales call. There’s always a million things I want to do, and that’s the problem.
If I don’t stop and ask what I don’t want to do, I’ll just keep doing everything until I’m exhausted, and that’s not a good way to live. So what don’t I want to do? I don’t want to write a blog post. I don’t want to answer 20 emails. I don’t want to think about the taxes. And I definitely don’t want to sit in front of my screen until 10 PM, which is what would happen if I didn’t consciously decide to stop doing things at some point.
“Wow. That’s a good question,” Michael said. “I’ll have to think about that one!”
If you’re an ambitious person, a creative, or an entrepreneur, you too are probably already overflowing with things you want to do. So instead of adding more fuel to the fire, why don’t you ask what you don’t want to do?
When you’re excited about your work, saying no is the hardest but most important thing you’ll do. It’s easy to get carried away, to spend all your time on something you love, and to forget there’s more to life than just that one thing. Sometimes, it takes a good question to remember.

### Title: The Perfect, Imperfect Filter

### Content: 
In the two and a half hours we hung out, Michael and I talked about everything under the sun: work, blockchain, productivity, parenting, self-care, writing, creativity, and on and on. One particularly noteworthy topic? Note-taking.
I’m a big believer in note-taking. Always have been. I’ve taken notes in school, taken notes in college, and I take notes at work. I take notes when I read, and I take notes in meetings. I take notes from my own thoughts and ideas, and I take notes when I talk to people.
Michael, on the other hand, is a believer in “ the perfect, imperfect filter: ” the human brain. “I’ve never taken notes in my life, and I’ve done just fine,” he said. “Everything I need to remember, I remember. Everything else, I don’t.”
Michael is a smart guy. He has a PhD. He is a professor at a prestigious school. He has published a million papers. And he runs a company with thousands of employees. Clearly, his filter is working. If he had taken notes, he might have done better still. But he did extremely well regardless.
What I learned from this is that there are many ways to solve any one problem. Some people take notes. Some people don’t. Some people remember everything. Others don’t. Some people are visual learners. Others are more conceptual.
The only way to find out what works for you is to keep an open mind. Try different approaches. Listen to what other people do. What works for them may not work for you, but it’s good to know what’s out there. Keep trying until you find what fits, and then keep adapting as you go.
It’s okay to be different. Just because someone does something you don’t doesn’t make either one of you wrong. You’re two people, each with their own habits, beliefs, and attitudes. What you share is a problem, and how you choose to solve it is up to you.
The next time you catch yourself thinking, “I wish I could do that,” remember: You can’t — but you also don’t have to. You have your own way of doing things, and if it works for you, that’s all that matters.

### Title: Working Titles

### Content: 
Every time I see the words on the big screen again, I marvel at the brilliance behind the name: “a Working Title production.” Working Title is one of Britain’s most successful movie studios ever, the company behind films like Love Actually, Darkest Hour, and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, among many others. Making their own name one that would forever remain in progress didn’t just make for great marketing. It’s also a good reminder there’s always work left to be done.
Just like the studio’s name, so is everything else. From the moment we’re born, we’re working titles. Always in progress, never perfect. That’s the deal we’ve made, and we’re not gonna get a new one anytime soon.
We are working titles, and so are our relationships, our careers, and our possessions. Everything is in flux, and whatever is too good to be true probably is. The only true way to win is to keep playing, and the best way to play is to keep working.
It’s a humbling experience, this realization that we’re all drafts sent out to sea. But it’s also liberating. No more pressure to be perfect! No more need to get it right on the first try! It’s all a work in progress, and that’s exactly the way it’s meant to be.
Whether you’re a movie studio, a mother, or a musician, remember: You’re a working title — and there’s always something left to do.

### Title: What Are We Doing?

### Content: 
It’s a question that deserves asking. And often. Today at work, four people were discussing the specifics of a video I didn’t know we were creating, nor what for. So I asked: “What are we doing here?” No one had an answer, and if nothing else, it showed us: Perhaps we are trying to do too much.
We’re all busy, of course. Busy doing a lot of different things. But are those different things all part of one coherent effort? Or do we just do a little of everything, hoping some of it will add up? For the video, it turned out we were creating a new, more personal format, but no one had really thought through how it would fit into our overall content strategy. We’ve now decided to first run the idea by our boss.
What are we doing? It’s a question that extends beyond the confines of your workday. Why are you trying to get promoted? Why are you starting a podcast? Why are you writing a book? And it goes beyond even the borders of work altogether. Why are you hanging out with this person? Why are you moving to this city? Why are you buying a house?
“What are we doing?” It’s a simple question, but it’s one we can answer in countless ways. Some will be better than others. We won’t always have a great one, and we won’t always know the answer when we need it. But it’s still a question worth asking — and if we ask it often enough, it’ll keep us on track more so than we could ever imagine.

### Title: Keep Your Cool

### Content: 
Talking about not freaking out during major stock market declines in his 2017 annual shareholder letter, Warren Buffett suggested we remember a few select lines from a 19th-century poem by Rudyard Kipling, If :
 to keep your cool when all about you are losing theirs.
In the poem, Kipling talks about many other things, of course. He wants his son to be honest, fair, and not give up too soon. But when Buffett quotes him, he quotes the lines about keeping your head on straight when everyone else is losing theirs.
Perhaps, this is because that is Buffett’s main feat. The thing that, above all others, has contributed to his success. The reason why, as he notes, a 20-year-old with a 150 IQ who behaves rationally will do better in the markets than a 25-year-old with a 140 IQ who is often swayed by emotions.
I’m not a genius, but I do have a hunch about what Buffett might say about Kipling’s poem if asked about it in an interview: “It’s a great poem, but if I had to pick one line to remember, it’d be ‘If you can keep your head when all about you are losing theirs…’”
There is no such thing as a free lunch, but there is a free way to get ahead: Keep your cool.

### Title: Improving Without Criticism

### Content: 
George Lee may not have been part of Bruce Lee’s bloodline, but he was definitely family. As Bruce’s equipment manager—and, more importantly, maker —he forged dozens of specialized training items based on Bruce’s ideas and requests.
George would make wooden dummies for Bruce to practice on, a padded board to kick against, and even a device to measure one’s punching power. Bruce, in turn, would test all of these items in his daily training. If he found a flaw, he would go to George and say: “This needs to be improved.”
When Bruce died, George lost not just a friend but also his job. He returned to his normal life, and it would be decades until he next heard the words “this needs to be improved.”
After George retired, he became a member of a local hiking group. One day, he made a joke about his fellow hikers’ poor sense of direction. The group’s leader said: “This needs to be improved.” Immediately, George thought: “Ah! Bruce Lee!”
In an interview, George explains that, back in the day, he thought little of Bruce’s phrase. “It was just a normal thing. But when I heard it again, I realized it was actually a very special phrase.” Why? Because “Bruce never said anything was bad or anything was good. He just said, ‘This needs to be improved.'”
“Most people would say, ‘This is bad. You did this wrong.’ But Bruce would never say that. He would just say, ‘This needs to be improved.'”
What a wonderful way of looking at the world. No criticism, just opportunities to improve. No judgement, just ideas for change. Don’t condemn. Refine! That was Bruce Lee’s approach, and it’s as liberating as it is useful.
When you want to make something better, point at it and say: “This needs to be improved.” Whether you’re making a device, managing a team, or training to be a kung fu legend, that’s all there ever is to see—and all you’ll ever have to say.

### Title: Working for the Cat

### Content: 
After weeks of back and forth around a joint presentation, the CEO of the company we were in talks with left. Suddenly, there’s a new boss, a new team, and the whole process starts from scratch. I smiled when I saw the email. I don’t think my slides will go to waste. They can be amusing, the tides of time and business.
When I was younger, I would have been devastated. “Why is this happening to me?” I would have thought. “How could they do this to me?” But the truth is that no one did anything to me at all. Shit happens. People quit. Projects fail. Presentations get scrapped. It’s all part of life, and we’re not the center of it. We’re a small piece of a big puzzle, and if we don’t get to play our part, that’s perfectly okay.
I’m not perfect in this. I still have my moments. But I’ve learned to find comfort in a good old German idiom: “Die Katze muss man ja auch am Schwanz halten.” It translates roughly to “you also have to hold the cat by its tail” and means that, yes, there’s always something else that needs to be done. You didn’t expect to feed the cat today, but here we are. Your presentation got shelved, but that’s life! There’ll be another one tomorrow.
It’s good to feel sad when you lose something, but it’s even better to not take the loss so personally. We all serve many masters, and the cat is just one of them.

### Title: Knowing Too Much and Too Little

### Content: 
The more time he spends wandering through the Aiel Waste, a barren, desert landscape in the Wheel of Time universe, the more “Dragon Reborn” Rand al’Thor understands the extent of his powers. Powerful magic that’s bound to corrupt him, strength to withstand even strong enemies’ attacks, and unreliable but enlightening visions of the future—such are the burdens of the chosen one.
But the more Rand knows, the less he seems to trust in the very people he is supposed to lead and protect. He becomes suspicious of his friends and tries to do everything alone. “I know too much, and not enough,” he tells his Aiel bodyguard. “I don’t know who I can trust anymore. I don’t even know if I can trust myself.”
It’s true that knowledge corrupts, but it’s also a matter of knowing too much and too little at the same time. When we learn how to do our job, we might realize we’re no good at it. When we become an expert, we see how much more there is to know. And when we finally understand how a situation works, we’ll spot the many ways in which it could go wrong.
The trick is to not let knowledge erode your confidence. Don’t forget what you’ve always known, and don’t let the unknowns throw you off your game. Knowledge is power, but only if you don’t let it get to you.

### Title: Pretend It’s the Last Time

### Content: 
My sister once reminded me that there are plenty of last times we miss. The last time we hang out with a friend before our paths twist in separate directions. The last time we have a certain food before we leave a place we’ll never revisit. Sometimes, we might even fail to recognize the last phone call with someone we love before they die. That’s why “this might be the last time” is a thought worth having on occasion.
What’s less obvious but perhaps even more important, however, is pretending “this is the last time” when you know it’s not going to be. When you’re not sick of your friend but tired of talking about the same old stuff. When you’re not sick of the food but tired of eating it every day. And when you’re not sick of your job but tired of doing the same task over and over again.
Pretend it’s the last time you can ask your friend the most interesting question you can think of. Pretend it’s the last time you can eat your favorite dish. And pretend it’s the last time you can submit a report with a new idea for a change. Watch what happens. How will you approach the situation? Which emotions come up? Is there a tinge of nostalgia? Some relief? And how do you act? Are you more curious? More thorough? More creative?
Sometimes, it’s important to realize what you’re about to lose before it’s gone. At other times, you must remember what makes something worth keeping while you still have it. Don’t wait for the last time. Make the most of today.

### Title: Zero Copies

### Content: 
That’s how many I sold when I finally got my long-coveted Kindle Daily Deal.
After years of asking Amazon to promote my books, I finally got an email: “We would like to feature your book The 4 Minute Millionaire on October 15th, 2023.” I was thrilled! I set up the promotion, and I crossed my fingers.
Unfortunately, the deal didn’t go as I had imagined. Instead of being featured in the usual “Kindle Daily Deal” email, which goes out to millions of people, my book was tucked away on some remote page on Amazon, where only the most dedicated bargain hunters would ever find it. As a result, I sold zero copies.
It was a good reminder that, ultimately, your marketing is your responsibility. You can’t outsource it. You can’t hand it off to someone else and expect them to do a good job. You have to bring people to your work. You have to make them care. And you have to do it every day.
Sure, on some days, you’ll sell zero copies. But if you keep going, sooner or later, you’ll sell one — and that’s how it all begins.

### Title: It’s Your Response-Ability

### Content: 
Sometimes, a word transforms completely when you see it not for its dictionary entry but for its parts. Will Smith is a master at this. So was Bruce Lee. In Striking Thoughts, he notes that “response-ability” is one of several synonyms for “living in the now” and leaning into your creativity.
We are not mere bystanders, Bruce wrote. We are actors. Participants. “Man is always a participant in the creative process, not by his mere existence, but by the nature of his reaction to the present.” It is our response-ability that makes us human. It is our ability to respond that makes us human.
It is not a duty. It is not a burden. It is a privilege. We have the ability to respond, and we can do so in infinite ways. We can choose to respond with anger. We can choose to respond with sadness. We can choose to respond with humor, with creativity, with kindness, with empathy, and with patience. We can choose to respond with a smile, with a nod, with a shrug, with a laugh, and with a hug. We can choose to respond with words, with silence, with a song, with a dance, and with a prayer. We can choose to respond with action, with waiting, with thinking, with learning, and with practicing.
Whatever the situation, the choice is ours. We can choose to respond to everything, to nothing, and to something in between. We can choose to respond now, to respond later, and to respond never. But we can always choose to respond. That is our response-ability, and it is ours to exercise as we see fit.
Life is not something that happens to us. We are not mere victims, floating down the river of time. We are paddlers in our own canoe. We are the ones steering the ship. The question is will we grab the oars? Will we take the wheel? Will we take responsibility for our response-ability?
The only way to find out is to ask us. You know where we are. We’re right here. Living in the now, exercising our response-ability. And we’ll do it again tomorrow. Care to join us?

### Title: Still Water Is a Mirror

### Content: 
“Moving, be like water. Still, be like a mirror.” That’s one of Bruce Lee’s Striking Thoughts. When I read it, I realized that, actually, this is an encouragement to be like water, period.
What does a mirror do? It reflects. It reacts to whatever is placed in front of it. The moment the object moves, the mirror changes. That’s what water does too. It adapts to whatever vessel it is poured into. It is always moving, changing, flowing from one state to another, from one place to another. But if you put it into a glass and let it sit, it will also just sit. It will wait until it is needed.
Still water is a mirror, and so are we. We are not meant to be moved by everything. Sometimes, the best thing we can do is to stay still. To wait and reflect. To be a mirror. Only when the right inputs come along can we mirror them back in the right direction. When we react to the wrong things, we’ll only send them right back from whence they came. That’s not helpful. It doesn’t move the energy along.
It takes time to learn what to reflect and what to absorb. To know when to stay still and when to move. But it is a skill worth learning. You are not a mirror. You are water. But when you are still, you are a mirror. It is a paradox, but it is one worth remembering.

### Title: Don’t Give Up in Anger What You Started in Love

### Content: 
The Silo is a dangerous place. 10,000 people cooped up in a 144-floor concrete pillar at all times, with no access to the outside? That’s a recipe for disaster even on the best of days. But once people start dying under mysterious circumstances, all bets are off.
In the world of Wool, the only world that’s left, the sheriff is the highest authority in the Silo. He must solve crimes, keep the peace, and, most of all, maintain hope. When he suddenly retires, his deputy must take his place. But she can’t possibly fill his shoes, and so the spiral of doom only gets worse from there.
At one point in the story, the deputy-turned-sheriff, Juliette, gets a message from her predecessor. “I’m sorry I left you,” Holston says. “I didn’t know what else to do.” Having just lost her boyfriend, Juliette is furious. She wants to throw Holston’s note into the fire, but something stops her. “What was that?” she wonders. “Pride? Or was it fear? Maybe it was both.”
Juliette realizes that Holston, too, was scared. Scared of what he didn’t know, scared of the world, and scared of losing his wife. “He had given up in anger what he’d started in love,” Juliette concludes. That’s why he left. That’s why he quit. “And now, he was sorry.”
There’s a lot to be said about the Silo, about fear, and about love. But right now, I’d just like to point out that, yes, it’s true: It’s easy to abandon things when we’re angry, even when we began them with the best intentions and the noblest of desires.
It’s easy to quit your job when your boss yells at you. It’s easy to break up with someone when they hurt your feelings. And it’s easy to throw the guitar into the closet when your fingers are sore from pressing strings. But what good will any of that do? What purpose does it ultimately serve?
Sometimes, the easiest thing is also the right thing. Most of the time, however, it is not. Usually, the easiest thing is only a distraction. A quick fix for a problem that requires a long-term solution. An immediate band-aid on a wound that needs to be healed with slow, careful treatment.
Don’t give up in anger what you started in love. Take a break. Cool off. Return to the problem with a clear head, and chances are, you’ll see it’s not as big as it looks. You’ll find a way to move forward. To keep the peace, solve the crime, and, most of all, maintain hope.

### Title: Flick It Again

### Content: 
We have a big cuddle blanket on our couch. It’s massive. Two by two meters or so. In the winter, we use it every night, and every morning, I fold it back into shape.
’t as easy as folding a normal blanket. This thing is heavy, and it takes a lot of work to get it back into a square shape. Yesterday, I thought: “What if I just flick it?”
I held the blanket in the middle, raised it, and shook it. It flapped about a bit, but it also straightened itself out. I did it again, and again, and eventually, I managed to fold it with much less effort than I usually need.
Sometimes, you don’t need a new approach. You need a new angle. A different perspective. What if you look at your problem from the top? What if you turn it sideways? Can you see it in the mirror? Or through your friend’s eyes? Perhaps you can even flick it, and it’ll straighten itself out.
Don’t give up too early. Flick it again.

### Title: An Eternity for a Steppenwolf

### Content: 
A “Steppenwolf” is a kind of wolfhound, half wild animal, half domesticated pet. In Hermann Hesse’s novel of the same name, protagonist Harry claims to be a specimen of this very variety, forever torn between a life outside society’s expectations and the comfort of hiding his lofty ideals in plain sight: among pubs, discussions about politics, and everything else mundane.
When he first meets his guide, a woman named Hermine, Harry explains that his “wolf,” the artist, the thinker, the dreamer, has long been dead. He is nothing but a husk, a ghost wandering the streets at night. “Not quite,” Hermine says. “Your wolf is not dead, he’s just lost in the forest. And he’ll come out of it just fine.”
Later in the book, Harry will indeed find his way back to art, love, and life. But first, he must pass many trials and tribulations. One of the most interesting is a conversation with a man named Pablo, who introduces him to the Magic Theater. “The price of admission is merely your own life,” Pablo says. “The theater happens to be the representation, the reflection, of life itself.”
In the theater, Harry finds many strange rooms, each with its own theme, like “All Girls Are Yours” or “Every Man for Himself.” In one room, he finds a book called “Treatise on the Steppenwolf.” In it, an unnamed author explains that “every human being has a thousand other humans inside,” and that most people, most of the time, are only aware of a small fraction of them. They live their lives in the company of a few dozen alter egos, and that is why they feel so trapped in their roles as husbands, wives, mothers, fathers, teachers, and accountants.
The Steppenwolf, however, is different. He can feel the whole choir of characters inside him, and it drives him mad. “A man of the cultivated classes today does not light-heartedly turn a somersault if his stomach hurts. Nor does he believe, as a man did in the past, that if he has a headache he can take a powder and his trouble will be over. A man of culture no longer has the firm, sound stomach he needs in order to be able to stand up to a pain when he has one. His refined nerves demand continual gratification; his sensibility requires them; and so, with his woolly heart, his fluttery soul, and his vague, clouded intellect, the refined, cultivated individual has no choice but to go to his doctor. The doctor appears, therefore, as an evil deity of sinister majesty; and the suffering soul has no means of defense against him.”
In other words, the Steppenwolf is so aware of his inner and outer conflicts, he can no longer turn a blind eye to them. And so, instead of living his life, he spends most of his time worrying about it. “I am in a constant state of contradiction,” Harry admits earlier in the book. “My ‘thou shalt’ is as strong as my ‘I want.’” The author in the book, meanwhile, has a response to Harry’s plight: “The Steppenwolf is a man of the cultivated class, and he therefore enjoys a very considerable and altogether illusionary feeling of freedom. He feels capable of determining, for himself and by himself, what he is and what he is not. To a great extent he has freed himself from the conventions of manners and customs. He does not feel bound, for example, to use a table fork or a table knife when eating, and he goes to the theater or attends a lecture in his dressing gown and slippers if he feels like doing so. But in all essential matters, he has no more freedom than a savage in a primeval forest.”
The Steppenwolf may feel superior to his more restrained, less self-aware peers, but actually, he is just as trapped as they are, perhaps even more so. He knows every rule in the book, and he sees no way of escaping from any of them. “The Steppenwolf would like to live for once without self-torture,” the author continues. “He would like to say: ‘I am not a thinking man, therefore I do not wish to think. I do not wish to carry the burden of thought. It is too heavy for me. I want henceforth to be a man without thought.’ But alas! The Steppenwolf cannot do this. He cannot cease from thinking, for his brain will not leave him in peace. His thinking is not good for much, but it is his life.”
And then, the author drops the real hammer: “The Steppenwolf is not to be cured, for his disease is to be a Steppenwolf.”
If you are a Steppenwolf, you will spend your entire life torn between two or more opposing forces. You will never find lasting relief, let alone definitive answers. You will be a thinker until the day you die, and you will never stop doubting your own conclusions. But you will also never be bored. You will never lack inspiration, ideas, or a new perspective to try on. You will always have something to think about, to mull over, to occupy yourself with. You will be a seeker until the end, and even if you’ll never find everything you are looking for, you will always have a new trail to blaze, a new path to follow.
In the end, Harry finds his way back to life. He loses his love, but he finds a new home, a new place to call home. He is a Steppenwolf through and through, and he will be until his last day on earth. But he is also a human being, and that means he must live his life one day at a time. There are joys to be had, and there are sorrows to be felt. There are people to meet and things to be done.
If you are a Steppenwolf, you will spend an eternity in your own mind. But that eternity will fly by like a second. There will be no time to worry about the meaning of life. There will only be a life to live, and you will be too busy living it to realize it has already passed you by.
Don’t worry about tomorrow. Don’t worry about your contradictions. Live your life. Think your thoughts. Be a Steppenwolf. And tomorrow will take care of itself.

### Title: Life Is Not a Simulation

### Content: 
The movie Sully deals with the complications of becoming a hero. To the public, the situation was obvious: Chesley Sullenberger landed a jet plane with no functioning engines on the Hudson river and saved 155 people’s lives—give the man a medal, and let’s be grateful for some good news.
 what the media and the public did. The National Transportation Safety Board, however, was not so sure. In their eyes, Sully might have made a mistake. What if landing at an airport would have been the better option? What if he could have saved more people? Or saved everyone by taking a different path?
In order to find out, they ran simulations. They put Sully and his co-pilot into a machine, and they let them try again. They changed the starting conditions, and they asked: “What if?” They moved the plane 2,000 feet up in the air. They gave it another 90 seconds of runway. And they let the computers calculate the odds.
As it turns out, the simulations showed Sully could have made it to the airport. He would have saved everyone. In the real world, the NTSB now had a problem. If they publicly declared Sully a hero, they’d look like fools. If they told everyone he made a mistake, they’d look like fools. So they did what any government agency does in that situation: They tried to pin the blame on Sully.
The man, however, was too smart for their game. He had lived the situation. He knew what it was like. The NTSB had only seen the data. They had only run simulations. In the end, Sully got the better of them.
“Computer simulations are only as good as the data you put into them,” he said. “You can’t put a human life into a simulation.”
A plane is a machine, but the people piloting it are not. They must use their wits, their creativity, and their gut. A computer can’t factor those in, and that’s why simulations will never be perfect.
The same applies to life. We have all kinds of models and projections and forecasts, but in the end, we must live every day as it comes. We can’t fast-forward to the end and look at the results. We can only do our best, and we must trust that, like Sully, we’ll land safely in the Hudson when we need to.
Life is not a simulation. Don’t run through it in your head. Live it.

### Title: Appreciate the Basics

### Content: 
Today, our apartment has no water for eight hours. The irony? Outside, it’s raining all day long. But there’s a difference between water coming out of the sky or the ground and fresh H2O pouring out of your tap, and you only realize how big of a difference it is when you’re left without your usual conveniences.
I’m lucky. I have a large bottle of water in my fridge. I can still make coffee. I can brush my teeth at work. I can take a shower there too. But it’s not the same, is it? Not as practical. Not as efficient. And that’s why we pay for these things. It’s easy to forget, but actually, we should appreciate the basics every day.
Don’t wait for your internet to break, your phone to die, or your water to stop flowing. Thank your everyday miracle devices every time you use them.

### Title: Relevant Notifications

### Content: 
When the Pokémon hype gets real, trying to buy new card sets throws me right back to the 90s. Except instead of driving to a store on release day, hoping to get some product, I’m checking various Discord servers and online shops ten times a day. “Is it live yet?” Naturally, I often end up missing the five-minute window in which listings go up and immediately sell out.
Yesterday, I finally set up a notification on one of the channels I was monitoring. I thought I was doing myself a favor. Instead, I spent the rest of the day checking my phone every five minutes. “What’s the alert for? Is it relevant? Is it a mistake? Or something else entirely?”
In a world where information is always available, we think we need to know everything right away. But just because we can be always up to date does not mean we should be. “Better to stay ignorant,” my friend Mike says. “Relevant notifications are the best notifications,” I would add.
I can check my email once a day and still address anything urgent. I can look at the news at 6 PM and still know what’s important. And I can buy my cards a few weeks later and still pay a fair price.
Don’t drown in information just because you can. Be selective in what you allow to trigger you, and stay focused on what matters.

### Title: Ride the Schoolbus

### Content: 
The first train connection from my parents’ house to a larger city where I transfer runs through the middle of nowhere. The second stop is a town with a school. Often, many kids get on the tiny, two-wagon train. So for the next 40 minutes, I’ll sit there, tucked away quietly between three dozen high schoolers, listening to their laughter and conversations. I always learn something.
Sometimes, I’ll hear them talk about their relationships, about music, or about sports. I’ll hear them complain about their parents, about school, and about life. But I’ll also hear them say, “I’m proud of you for sticking with it,” “You did a good job,” and “I think you should go for it.”
Most of all, I’ll hear them say, “I don’t know.” They’ll admit that they don’t know, and then, together, they’ll try to figure things out. Teenagers know very little about life, and they’re not ashamed to admit it. They’re not afraid to say “I don’t know.” They’re not worried about looking stupid. They’re too busy trying to figure out the world, and they’re doing it together. They’re not alone, and they know it.
In fact, they’re not alone at all. They’re on a bus full of people going the same direction, and if everyone chips in, everyone will benefit. It’s a wonderful thing, this camaraderie, and it’s something we tend to lose as we get older. Our connections become more individual. We no longer go to school together. We go to work, and work is a different kind of place. It’s not as easy to admit that you don’t know. It’s not as natural to be curious. And it’s not as fun to be on a journey together.
But that’s what life is, isn’t it? A journey. A trip on the school bus. We’re not alone. We never were. We’re all figuring out life together. Let’s admit that we don’t know. Let’s be curious. Let’s share our stories, our laughter, and our complaints. Let’s be proud of each other. Let’s cheer each other on. And let’s ride the school bus together.

### Title: The 3 Kinds of Eternity

### Content: 
Harry, the antihero of Hermann Hesse’s Steppenwolf, suffers a prolonged, fundamental identity crisis. One idea that gives him comfort is the concept of eternity, which various supporting characters define anew for him in illustrious ways.
 one of those characters, Harry learns that, actually, there are several kinds of eternity, and they all differ quite a bit from one another.
The first kind of eternity is the eternity we know from our calendars. It is the eternity of time, and it is nothing more than a theoretical construct. “If you take an hour and add another hour to it, and then add another hour, and so on endlessly, you will never reach eternity,” Harry is told. “And yet eternity consists of hours.”
The second kind of eternity is the eternity of space. “If you take a yard and add another yard to it, and so on forever, you will never reach eternity. And yet eternity consists of yards.”
The third kind of eternity is the eternity of the soul. “If you take a thought and add another thought to it, and so on forever, you will never reach eternity. And yet eternity consists of thoughts.”
If you ask me, only one of these eternities is worth pursuing: the eternity of the soul. If we spend our lives chasing the infinity of time, we’ll never get off the treadmill. We’ll forever worry about the hours left to us, and we’ll always be thinking about the next thing we must do to fill them. What if those hours were eternal? It’d be a never-ending nightmare.
The same applies to the infinity of space. More stuff, more experiences, more places to see — if we don’t turn off the music on this infinite mixtape, it’ll only drive us insane. What if we had infinite time to see infinite space? That’d be the perfect prison.
The infinity of the soul, however, is an entirely different game. If we add one thought to another thought, and then another, and then another, we can create a never-ending, ever-evolving picture of our true self. We can become the best version of ourselves, and then we can reinvent that version. We can do it again and again, forever. We can do it for as long as we live, and if we do, we’ll live eternally.
When we think of eternity, we tend to think of the vastness of time and space, but that’s not what it’s truly about. It’s about the vastness of the human spirit. The infinity of the soul is the only kind of eternity worth chasing, and it is, thankfully, the one that’s within reach.
Don’t waste your life fretting about the minutes and miles. Think. Imagine. Create. Turn your thoughts into a never-ending staircase, and you’ll ascend to the highest heights.

### Title: Two Hamsters in the Background

### Content: 
We had some friends over for coffee and cake. Instead of just playing music from a speaker, I put on a lo-fi mix on our TV. Like most music videos of this kind, it featured a drawn wallpaper image. In the background, there were two cute hamsters, sitting, sipping tea from their cups.
’t one point, our friend looked at the TV and said: “Oh, those two hamsters are so cute!” I’m not sure what I would have done if the video had just been music, but since it was so visually focused, I ended up looking at the screen quite a bit. I, too, thought the hamsters were cute. I also thought about how the video had evolved over time, and how it differed from other lo-fi videos.
What I didn’t think about was the question our friend asked next: “How much of this stuff does he even remember?” “He” was me, and “this stuff” was a long to-do list for our new home that I had written down a few days before. It was a good question. I was able to recall everything from memory.
If you had asked me whether I could remember the list before our friend brought it up, I’d have said, “I don’t know, but probably not all of it.” Yet as soon as she made the list the focus of the conversation again, I could easily recall everything. It was as if the list had been sitting in my subconscious all along, waiting for its turn to be needed.
It’s a good skill to be able to recall things on command, but it’s also comforting to know that your brain can file away whatever it needs to file away, and you don’t have to worry about what you can and can’t remember. Your brain will give you what you need when you need it.
It’s okay if you can’t recall every detail of every meeting. It’s okay to not know where you put your keys. Your brain is a never-ending story — and if you ask me, two hamsters in the background are the perfect companions for the journey.

### Title: Delete the Adjectives, Get the Facts

### Content: 
Cool-headed as she is, Scout Finch cannot escape every trap life sets for any child growing up with a four years older brother. By the time Jem hits sixth grade, he actually gets interested in what school has to offer. Unfortunately for Scout, whatever he learns he blows out of proportion when relaying it to her.
One day, he tells her that “dignity” is a lady sitting on a chair, and the next, he claims “tolerant” is a person’s picture in the dictionary. Naturally, Scout is annoyed. She tells him to stop talking nonsense, and, after a brief spat, they go to bed.
The next morning, Atticus Finch, their father, finds his two children in the kitchen. He asks them how they slept, and Scout tells him: “Well, Jem and I had a big fight last night, and I don’t want to talk to him ever again.” Atticus asks what the fight was about, and Scout says: “Jem says you aren’t rich, but he says you’re white.”
Now, as a black man in a town full of white people, Atticus can’t help but laugh. “No, I’m afraid not, Scout,” he says. “He’s just a country lawyer, honey. We can’t afford a cook.” “Well, Jem says you’re white anyway,” Scout goes. “How can you be rich and not be white?”
At this point, Atticus knows it’s time to step in. “We just are, Scout. We just are.” “Then why don’t rich people like us live in fine houses like the Cunninghams do? They like to live like we do, out in the country.” “Because they have to pay a cook and all, just like we don’t. You know how President Roosevelt goes around in a wheelchair and he can’t walk? Well, he tried to get us out of the depression by borrowing lots of money from the banks. Now the banks don’t have money, and the farmers don’t have money, and we don’t have money. That’s why we can’t have a cook.”
“Are we as poor as the Cunninghams?” “Not exactly, but almost,” Atticus says. “Then why do you go to church with them?” “Because they’re like us, honey. We don’t have Negroes and Polish people, except in the court system. We just have our kind of folks, and they like to keep away from the Cunninghams as much as they do the rest of us.”
This is a scene from Go Set a Watchman, a sequel to the famous novel To Kill a Mockingbird. Atticus Finch is a lawyer in a small town in Alabama. He defends a black man accused of raping a white woman, and his children, Jem and Scout, are trying to make sense of the world.
The scene above is a beautiful example of how, when we are children, we often add adjectives to the facts we receive, adjectives that don’t belong there. In this case, the adjectives are “rich” and “white.” Scout’s big takeaway from Jem’s lesson is that “you have to be rich to be white.” Atticus, however, knows that’s not true. He must delete the adjectives to get to the facts, and then he must help his daughter do the same.
Scout is confused because she has added her own interpretation to the facts. She has created a false equivalence, and now, it is up to Atticus to break it down. Atticus must explain that, yes, there are rich people, and there are white people, but being rich does not automatically make you white, nor does being white automatically make you rich. The two are not connected, no matter how much we might wish they were.
It is easy for children to fall into this trap. They are still learning how to process the world, and so they often jump to conclusions. They see a pattern and assume it holds everywhere, even when it doesn’t. But as we grow up, we must learn to delete the adjectives. We must learn to get to the facts.
When you are a child, it is easy to believe that the world is simple. You see things in black and white, and you think that’s how they are. But as you grow up, you realize that the world is not so simple. There are shades of gray, and there are things you don’t understand.
It is easy to want to go back to the simplicity of childhood. To want to believe that the world is still black and white. But that’s not the way it works. The world is complex, and we must learn to live with that complexity. We must learn to delete the adjectives and get to the facts.
The next time you find yourself adding adjectives to the facts, stop. Take a breath. And then, delete the adjectives. Get to the facts. It won’t always be easy, but it will always be worth it.

### Title: The Water Cathedral of Identity

### Content: 
Modern books are often littered with testimonials. My copy of Der Steppenwolf by Hermann Hesse needs just one: “There are only few books which transform us, which give us courage to change our lives,” French writer Frederic Beigbeder says on the back cover. “ Der Steppenwolf is one such book.”
It’s a book about identity, and it starts with an intriguing image: A man walks through the streets of a nameless city at night, and he sees a puppet show. In the display window, a little theater is set up, and on its stage, a human-sized wolf stands on his hind legs, dressed in tails. He wears a top hat, and he looks around as if he’s lost. “Steppenwolf,” the label reads, and the wolf is indeed a lonesome animal in the desert of civilization.
The man watching the show is fascinated. He studies the wolf in detail. He sees the wolf’s claws and teeth, and he spots the wounds on his face. The wolf has survived a lot, it seems. But he has also shed a lot of blood. As the man is about to move on, a card falls from the sky. It’s part of the display, but it catches the man off guard. “Magic Theater,” it reads. “Not for everybody.” It also says that the theater will show him “the horrors of hell” and “the joys of heaven.” Intrigued, the man pockets the card and goes about his day.
Later that day, the man stumbles into a bookstore. He is looking for a book, and the owner, too, reminds him of a wolf. The man finds the book, and the owner presents him with a small treat: A little, leather-bound booklet, full of strange aphorisms. It is the second half of the magic show, and it prompts the man to ask the owner about the card. The owner only shrugs, and the man leaves the store.
As he continues to walk, the man is now fully engrossed in the book. He reads it on the street, reads it in the park, and reads it at home. It is a book about a man who is fascinated by a puppet show. A man who finds a card for a magic theater, and who receives a little, leather-bound booklet from a book store owner. The man in the book is named Harry Haller, and he is the Steppenwolf. The man reading the book is named Hermann Hesse, and he is the author of the story.
You might be wondering: What is going on? I was. I am. But I think the answer is as simple as it is mind-bending: This is a story about identity. A story that can only be told in the format it is told in. A story that must be lived to be understood. That’s why Hesse had to write it. That’s why you and I had to read it. And that’s why it is one of the few books that transforms us.
Identity is like a cathedral made of water. It’s a structure so complex, so multi-faceted, so infinitely faceted, really, it can only be comprehended in its entirety when we look at it from the outside. The problem with identity, however, is that we can never look at it from the outside. We are born right into the center of it, and we spend our lives trying to understand it from the inside out. It’s a bit like being born inside a maze, and it’s as hard as it sounds.
Hesse’s book is a maze, too. A maze of mirrors. As you read it, you see yourself everywhere. You’re the Steppenwolf. You’re the reader. You’re the book store owner. You’re the author. You’re the person who made the puppet show. You’re the one handing out the cards. You’re even the little booklet with the aphorisms. You’re everywhere, and yet, you’re nowhere at all. Because you’re not just all of these characters. You’re also the reader. The person holding the book. The observer. The one looking in from the outside. And that’s the magic of it.
By constructing this never-ending mirror maze, Hesse has elevated us. He has lifted us out of our identity and placed us on the outside. We can now look at ourselves from afar. We can see our lives from a new angle, and we can finally understand something about the totality of ourself that we could never have understood before. It’s a magical experience, and that’s why the book is called Der Steppenwolf.
The book has many interpretations. It’s a book about finding yourself. It’s a book about losing yourself. It’s a book about art, about life, and about love. It’s a book about everything and nothing at all. But most of all, it’s a book about identity. That’s why it’s one of the few books that transforms us. One of the few books that gives us the courage to change our lives.
The next time you see a puppet show, pay attention. You might find a card for a magic theater. It won’t be for everybody, but if you’re willing to venture inside, you may see the horrors of hell and the joys of heaven. You may even find yourself.

### Title: A Circle of Teaching

### Content: 
Yesterday, I showed my fiancée a bratwurst stall that I used to go to as a child when we went shopping in a certain town. Fresh rolls, lightly charred sausages—still a classic! After the salesman handed over the goods, I looked around for ketchup and mustard. I conveniently found them beside the stall.
I was about to pour some ketchup on my roll when my girlfriend stopped me: “Wait! That’s mayo, not ketchup!” I looked again at the bottle, and indeed, it was Heinz mayonnaise, not Heinz ketchup. “Huh. That’s weird. I could have sworn this was red. Maybe I’m just color-blind.”
We continued to joke about it, and I ended up putting both mayo and ketchup on my roll, which was delicious. But as I was chewing on my first bite, I realized: “Wait a minute! The ketchup was red. It just came out of a red tube!”
In Germany, ketchup usually comes in small, portion-sized portions. It’s a bit of plastic that looks like a tiny toothpaste tube, and you have to break off the top to get to the ketchup. When you squeeze it, red ketchup comes out. That’s what I had done, and that’s why the ketchup looked red to me. My girlfriend, however, was used to American ketchup, which comes out of a big glass bottle and is brown before it hits the air.
That’s a funny little incident, but it’s also a great example of how teaching works. I learned from my girlfriend that not all ketchup is red, and she learned from me that German ketchup is. We both taught each other something in a matter of seconds.
When you approach life as a student, you’ll never stop learning, and you’ll also never stop teaching. Everything you do will have a purpose, and everything you share will have value. You won’t always get the timing right, but you’ll always be part of a circle of teaching.
Stay humble, stay curious, and stay kind. You never know who might need your lesson —and you’re never too old to learn from those around you.

### Title: Amending Your Words

### Content: 
During his second year at Hogwarts, Dumbledore tells Harry Potter that “help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it.” And for the next five years, Harry operates under that mantra.
In the seventh and final installment of the series, however, the new headmaster of the school, Severus Snape, claims that Dumbledore’s words were “a mistake.” “Headmaster,” he says, “it is too late. He has made other plans. If you go there, he will know.” “Please,” Dumbledore says, “just this once.”
At first, Snape refuses to help, but eventually, he agrees. The scene is a powerful reminder: It’s never too late to amend your words. You can change your mind any time, and so can anyone else. Words are not set in stone, and neither are the people who speak them.

### Title: Good People

### Content: 
Those are the ones we seek, aren’t they? But what does “good” mean? Three examples, one lesson.
 The first time I heard about him, he was already gone. My dad’s best friend from school. He died in a car accident. He was only 23.
In my family, we’ve been calling him “the angel” ever since. He’s the angel now, looking out for us from above. I never met him, but I’ve always felt a little bit safer knowing he’s around.
The second time I heard about him, I learned that he was the reason we have the first-aid classes we have in Germany today. He was a paramedic and, together with his dad, helped push for better training in schools.
After he died, his parents set up a foundation in his name. To this day, they help people who want to volunteer as paramedics.
The third time I heard about him, my dad told me a story from when they were 17. One day, they were at a gas station, just hanging out. My dad was wearing a sweater with the logo of a car company on it. The guy at the desk asked him: “Oh, do you drive one of those?”
My dad said: “No, I’m just wearing it because I like the sweater.” The guy said: “Oh, you can’t do that. You’ll have to pay 50 Deutschmark.” Back then, that was about 25 bucks, which, for a 17-year-old, is a lot of money.
My dad said: “What? That’s ridiculous. I’m not paying. I’ll just take off the sweater.” The guy said: “Okay, then I’ll call the police.” My dad said: “You can’t call the police. This is stupid. I’m leaving.”
As he turned around and walked out the door, he heard his best friend say: “I’ll pay.” And he just put 50 Deutschmark on the counter and walked out the door.
I don’t know if my dad ever paid him back, but I do know this: That was a good person.
The first time I heard about her, I was already in love. I couldn’t tell you why. Maybe it was the smile. Maybe it was the eyes. Or the laugh. All I know is I was hooked.
The second time I heard about her, I learned that she was a singer. She was in a band. They played at lots of events and weddings. Sometimes, they even sang in church.
The third time I heard about her, I learned that she was a teacher. She taught elementary school kids. She was their favorite. They all loved her so much. They still talk about her today.
The fourth time I heard about her, I learned that she had died. I cried my eyes out. I didn’t know her, but it still hurt. I still loved her. She was my angel.
The fifth time I heard about her, I learned that she had done what I was about to do. She had moved to another country. She had gone to America. She had followed her dream.
I don’t know if I’ll ever stop missing her, but I do know this: She was a good person.
The first time I heard about him, I was in awe. I had never met anyone who worked so hard. He was always running. Always thinking. Always doing something. I wanted to be just like him.
The second time I heard about him, I realized that, even though he worked a lot, he never seemed stressed. He was always calm. Always cool. Always collected. I wanted to be just like him.
The third time I heard about him, I understood that, even though he was always busy, he was never too busy to help. He was always there for his friends. Always willing to listen. Always happy to give advice. I wanted to be just like him.
The fourth time I heard about him, I learned that, even though he was successful, he never bragged about it. He never told people to get things. He never asked for favors. He just kept his head down and kept working. I wanted to be just like him.
The fifth time I heard about him, I noticed that, even though he was successful, he never stopped learning. He never stopped trying. He never stopped growing. I want to be just like him.
I don’t know if I’ll ever live up to his example, but I do know this: He is a good person.
Good people come in all shapes and sizes. They’re not all angels. They’re not all singers. They’re not all hardworking. But they’re always kind. They’re always generous. They’re always willing to help.
We all have a different picture of what “good” means, but I think if you can name three examples, you’re on the right track. I think if you can tell three stories, you get what it’s about.
Good people are all around us. They might be our best friends, our neighbors, or our coworkers. They might be gone before we ever meet them, or long gone before we ever realize.
But they’re always there, and that’s why, even though it’s not always easy, it’s important we try to be good people.

### Title: Infinity and Eternity

### Content: 
Infinity asked his sister Eternity: “Do you ever get bored?” “All the time,” Eternity said. “How about you?”
“Sometimes, I wish I was finite,” Infinity said. “But if I was, I’d only wish for eternity.”
“I wish there was something I could do for you,” Eternity said. “But if I could, I’d only wish for infinity.”
“Perhaps we’re just two sides of the same coin,” Infinity said. “Maybe, we’re one and the same.”
“Or maybe,” Eternity said, “we’re just brother and sister. Maybe, we should enjoy each other’s company.”
And for a while, Infinity and Eternity did just that.

### Title: Press “L” To Like

### Content: 
That’s the latest mechanism on Substack, a platform dedicated to email newsletters and those who like to read and write them. But what is it for?
Is it for the creators? After all, it’s nice to get a thumbs up every once in a while. But if you can’t see how many you get, nor who gave them to you, nor even the total number of likes, what good are they? Well, you can see who liked what, but unless someone likes your entire archive of 300 posts, that’s not very useful either.
Is it for the readers? It’s nice to be able to show appreciation, but if you can’t do it publicly, that too is worth only so much. “You liked this. That’s nice. I’m glad you liked it.” End of interaction. No comments. No discussion. Just a quiet nod in the wind.
Actually, I think “L” is for “love.” Love for the craft. Love for the reader. And love for the platform.
When you press “L,” nothing happens. The screen doesn’t change. There’s no animation. You don’t get a prompt. You don’t even get a sound. But if you click on the now green “L” again, it’ll turn white, and you’ll see a little checkmark appear. It’s subtle. Almost invisible. But it’s there. And that’s all you need.
If you’re a creator, you don’t need to know how many likes you got. You need to know that someone cared enough to like your work. If you’re a reader, you don’t need to start a conversation. You need to know you showed gratitude. And if you’re a platform, you don’t need to blow your own trumpet. You need to enable the people you serve to do their thing.
Substack is not a social media company. It’s a company for writers. Writers write. Readers read. And the “L” is for love.
Don’t expect fireworks for every good deed. Just keep pressing “L.”

### Title: It’s Still Chocolate

### Content: 
A few days ago, I miraculously got my hands on some original Dubai chocolate. A friend happens to live there, and his girlfriend kindly brought me a bar while she was in town. “Tell me what you think,” he texted me, “but I believe you and I will agree.”
I didn’t agree. The chocolate tasted bitter, and it was too crumbly. It also wasn’t creamy enough. “I think I prefer the German kind,” I told him. “But it’s still chocolate! And it’s nice to have a new kind.”
When you’re used to a certain standard, it’s easy to be disappointed when the same thing from a different place fails to live up. But even if it doesn’t live up, it’s still the same thing. It might not be as good, but it’s also not so bad as to not be worth trying. So don’t knock it till you’ve tried it, and don’t dismiss something different just because it’s not the same.
It’s still chocolate, and that makes it a special treat — even if it’s not the kind you’ll want to eat every day.

### Title: Chocolate for Breakfast

### Content: 
On some days, you’ll need it. Sure, you can sit there, moping, hoping your headache might disappear or that your metabolism will somehow magically kick into gear. Or, you can treat yourself when you need it the most and move on with your day.
Whether it’s a bar of chocolate, a cup of coffee, or a small glass of whiskey, the right dose of the right drug at the right time can make all the difference. Don’t be afraid to give yourself a break when you need one.

### Title: If You Want To Break Something, Use a Hammer

### Content: 
The Green Hornet is a superhero who’s been reinterpreted many times since his invention in 1936. Similar to Batman, he’s a wealthy publisher who fights crime as a masked vigilante at night. In a 1966 TV show edition, his sidekick and loyal driver, Kato, received a significant upgraded to his previously only alluded to martial arts skills. Why? Bruce Lee played the part.
As a result, Kato became a cult figure and Bruce Lee an international superstar. But what’s most interesting about this is how the show’s creators chose to portray Kato’s fighting skills. You might think they’d go to great lengths to explain them. To show the audience how he learned, where he learned, and how much. But they didn’t. They didn’t have to.
